blocks.x: NYC and NYS budget breakdowns relevant to CB6 and Brooklyn.

The city and state budget are among the most consequential policy documents produced each year. They determine what gets funded, what gets cut, and what the priorities of government actually are. This tab covers the NYC FY2027 executive budget and the NYS budget as they relate to CB6 and Brooklyn. Content will continue to grow as budget cycles progress.
FY2027 enacted budgets, in billions of dollars

New York State operates on a fiscal year running April 1 through March 31. The state uses an executive budget model: the Governor develops a comprehensive spending proposal, and the Legislature modifies and enacts it into law. With an enacted FY2027 budget of $268.5 billion, the state process directly shapes education funding, transportation capital, housing, and social services that flow into every community district.
The FY2027 state budget, step by step

blocks.d: By December 1, the Legislature and Judiciary submit their own funding requests to the Governor. The Governor is constitutionally required to include these figures unchanged in the Executive Budget — the separation of powers prevents the Governor from altering them.

The Governor opens the legislative session with the State of the State address, establishing policy priorities for the year. The Governor then submits the Executive Budget — by mid-January, or February 1 in a post-election year — along with appropriation bills and Article VII legislation.
Governor Hochul unveiled her FY2027 Executive Budget proposal on January 20, 2026.

Senate Finance and Assembly Ways and Means hold joint public hearings. Each chamber then independently develops a one-house budget. By March 1 the Executive and Legislature must hold a consensus revenue forecasting conference; if they fail to agree, the State Comptroller issues a binding forecast by March 5.
The NYS Assembly passed its one-house budget on March 10, establishing the chamber's spending priorities as an opening position for three-way negotiations with the Senate and Governor.
The NYS Senate passed its one-house budget resolution on March 12, establishing the chamber's spending priorities and opening position for three-way negotiations with the Assembly and Governor.

The Governor, Senate Majority Leader, and Assembly Speaker negotiate a final deal with three proposals on the table. Most discussions take place privately. Late budgets are common: New York has met its April 1 deadline in only about half of the past 40 years.

April 1 is the constitutional deadline and the start of the new state fiscal year. Once a deal is reached, both chambers vote on appropriation bills signed into law by the Governor. The Division of the Budget then issues an Enacted Budget Report. The FY2027 enacted budget totals $268.5 billion.

No deal was reached by April 1. The Governor and Legislature passed eleven extender bills to keep government funded while negotiations continued. Governor Hochul announced a general framework agreement on May 7, but Assembly Speaker Heastie disputed the deal was final. The budget was ultimately enacted on May 27, 2026 — 57 days past the deadline and the latest budget in 16 years.
Passed March 31. The Legislature passed a first budget extender through April 7, keeping state government funded while negotiations continue.
Governor Hochul signaled support for a pied-à-terre tax on high-value second homes as part of budget negotiations — a significant policy development with implications for housing and revenue.
Passed April 7. The Legislature passed a second budget extender through April 14.
Passed April 13. The Legislature passed a third budget extender through April 15.
Passed April 15. The Legislature passed a fourth budget extender through April 20.
Passed April 20. The Legislature passed a fifth budget extender through April 22.
Passed April 22. The Legislature passed a sixth budget extender through April 27.
Passed April 27. The Legislature passed a seventh budget extender through April 30, keeping state government funded while negotiations continue.
Passed April 29. The Legislature passed an eighth budget extender through Monday, May 4, keeping state operations and payroll funded while negotiations continue.
Passed May 4. The Legislature passed a ninth budget extender through Wednesday, May 6. Now more than a month past the April 1 deadline.

Passed May 7. The Legislature passed a tenth budget extender through Monday, May 11. Governor Hochul announced a general budget framework agreement that day, but Assembly Speaker Heastie disputed that a final deal was in place.

Passed May 11. The Legislature passed an eleventh budget extender through Thursday, May 14, keeping state operations funded including payroll, health programs, and unemployment insurance. 44 days past the April 1 deadline.
Passed May 14. The Legislature passed a twelfth budget extender through Monday, May 18, keeping state government funded while negotiations continued.

Passed Monday, May 18. The Legislature passed a thirteenth budget extender (S10520/A11445), worth roughly $8 billion and including close to $6 billion in school payments, funding the state through Wednesday, May 20. Senator José Serrano said lawmakers were closer than ever to a final deal. Extenders passed since April 1 had topped $31.7 billion.

Passed Wednesday, May 20. The Legislature passed a fourteenth budget extender (S10544/A11465) funding basic state obligations including payroll through Tuesday, May 26, and including $1.9 billion in new spending. The first full budget bill, debt service, had been the only one approved to that point.

Lawmakers passed the Education, Labor and Family Assistance and the Public Protection and General Government budget bills, both of which Governor Hochul signed the following Wednesday. Until May 20, debt service had been the only budget bill approved.

Coming off Memorial Day weekend, lawmakers passed the Transportation and Economic Development bill on May 26 — this cycle's "Big Ugly" omnibus — which Hochul signed soon after. The Assembly finished around 8 p.m. and the State Senate passed the final bill just before 11:30 p.m. Wednesday, May 27. Governor Hochul signed the remaining bills into law. The final spending plan is $268.5 billion — 57 days past the April 1 deadline and the latest enacted budget in 16 years. CB6-relevant provisions include a NYC pied-à-terre tax on luxury second homes, a J-51 tax abatement renewal through 2036, SEQRA reforms exempting many NYC housing projects from environmental review, a two-year extension of NYC mayoral control of schools, and authority for NYC to defer pension payments to help close its budget gap. Full enacted budget documents — including the Enacted Budget Financial Plan, appropriations, and school aid — are published by the NYS Division of the Budget.

New York City operates on a fiscal year running July 1 through June 30. The budget process spans nearly 12 months and involves community boards, borough presidents, the Mayor's Office of Management and Budget (OMB), and the City Council. Community boards are the first formal voice in that process — their district needs statements and budget requests set the foundation before the Mayor's Preliminary Budget is even released.
The FY2027 city budget, step by step

blocks.d: July 1 marks the start of the new fiscal year. Community boards immediately begin collecting resident input for the following year's budget — surveys, 311 data, and committee review all inform what gets submitted to the city.

Each of NYC's 59 community boards holds a public hearing, reviews community input, and votes on capital and expense budget priorities. The board submits a formal Statement of District Needs and Budget Requests to the Department of City Planning and OMB by November. CB6's district needs assessment documents priorities across Carroll Gardens, Cobble Hill, Columbia Waterfront, Gowanus, Park Slope, Red Hook.

OMB releases the November Financial Plan Update, the City's mid-year financial check-in. The November 2025 plan projected manageable gaps that the incoming Mamdani administration would later identify as significantly understated — driven by chronically underbudgeted shelter, rental assistance, and special education expenses.

Two weeks after taking office, Comptroller Mark Levine released his FY 2027 Budget Preview warning of a "remarkable" $12.6 billion budget gap across FY 2026 and FY 2027 — the largest fiscal strain since the Great Recession. Levine's analysis flagged optimistic revenue assumptions and chronically underbudgeted expenses inherited from the Adams administration.

Mayor Mamdani released a balanced $127 billion FY 2027 Preliminary Budget. The plan recognized $14 billion in previously underbudgeted city-funded agency expenses, deployed $1.77 billion in agency savings under new Chief Savings Officers (Executive Order 12), and assumed a 9.5% property tax rate increase ($3.7B) plus drawdowns from the Rainy Day Reserve Fund ($980M in FY26) and Retiree Health Benefit Trust ($229M in FY27). Mamdani identified raising income taxes on million-dollar earners and the most profitable corporations as the preferred path, requiring Albany authorization.

Community boards hold a public hearing on the Preliminary Budget and submit a letter of comment to OMB and the Department of City Planning. This is a second formal opportunity to press agencies on unmet budget requests and flag gaps in service delivery.

The City Council Finance Committee, chaired by Council Member Linda Lee, and other oversight committees begin agency-by-agency hearings on the Preliminary Budget. Council staff produce committee reports analyzing each agency's proposed spending against actual needs.

Speaker Menin and Finance Chair Linda Lee released the Council's March Economic and Tax Revenue Forecast, identifying nearly $1.7 billion in potential savings and additional revenue for FY 2026 — including $1.4 billion from debt service adjustments, accrual savings from unfilled vacancies, and unrecognized interest earnings. The analysis argued the City did not need to tap the Rainy Day Fund.

Speaker Menin and the City Council released a formal Preliminary Budget Response identifying $6 billion in resources to close the gap without raising property taxes, raiding reserves, or cutting services. Key proposals included $175 million in DOE contract savings, $80M in DOB construction permits, $42M in Port Authority rental revenue, plus expansion of Fair Fares and college savings accounts for kindergarteners. Mayor Mamdani sharply criticized the plan as "unrealistic."

Governor Hochul signaled support for a pied-à-terre tax on high-value second homes in NYC as part of state budget negotiations. The tax would become one of the central revenue tools available to the city, replacing the property tax increase in the eventual Executive Budget.

Mayor Mamdani and Speaker Menin issued a joint call for Albany to reduce the NYC Passthrough Entity Tax (PTET) credit to 75% and restore Aid and Incentives to Municipalities (AIM) funding (~$400M/year). Both leaders agreed to pass a city budget extender through May 12 to allow the FY2027 Executive Budget to incorporate the State's final budget decisions. Hochul publicly rejected the PTET ask the same day.

Mayor Mamdani released a $124.7 billion FY 2027 Executive Budget — a few billion less than the February Preliminary Budget. The plan closes the $5.4 billion gap without a property tax increase and without raiding reserves. Key changes: a new pied-à-terre tax on luxury second homes (~$500M), a reduced Unincorporated Business Tax credit (~$68M), $1.77B in agency savings, $202M from state takeover of line-of-duty death benefits, $600M in new youth programming, $300M in restored sales tax intercepts, and pension amortization potentially saving $2B+ over two years. Comptroller Levine commended the budget as "significantly improved" over February.

On the morning of the Executive Budget release, Governor Hochul and Mayor Mamdani jointly announced an additional $4 billion in gap-closing state support, bringing total new state assistance to nearly $8 billion over two years. The administration said the deal officially closes the more than $12 billion deficit it inherited. The agreement reframes the City-Albany relationship and pairs with the enacted state budget's NYC provisions, including the pied-à-terre tax and pension amortization authority.

The City Council holds a second round of public hearings, this time on the Executive Budget. Negotiations between the Council and the Mayor determine final funding levels. Community board requests that made it into agency responses carry the most weight here. The "handshake" deal between the Mayor and Speaker typically arrives in late June.

The City Council voted to adopt the FY2027 budget on June 30 — the charter deadline — with the adopted budget taking effect July 1. The Mayor and Council reached a handshake agreement on a roughly $126 billion budget (NYC's FY2026 adopted budget totaled $115.9 billion). Read the NYT coverage ↗ · Budget docs ↗
